questions.stem: A 45-year-old man without diabetes reports 6 months of morning confusion and blurred vision that resolve promptly after he eats; he has gained 8 kg from frequent snacking. During a documented spell, plasma glucose is 39 mg/dL with markedly elevated insulin, markedly elevated proinsulin, elevated C-peptide, and a negative sulfonylurea screen. Creatinine and liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulinoma of the pancreatic islet beta cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factitious use of injected pharmacologic insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factitious ingestion of a meglitinide such as repaglinide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alcohol-induced suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactive hypoglycemia from rapid intestinal absorption

explanation.summary: Elevated insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide with a negative drug screen during hypoglycemia indicates an insulinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulinomas are rare islet beta-cell tumors that release large amounts of insulin, so all markers of endogenous secretion rise together. Proinsulin at or above 5 pmol/L during laboratory-confirmed hypoglycemia supports endogenous hyperinsulinism, and the negative sulfonylurea screen excludes drug-stimulated secretion. Common causes such as antihyperglycemic drugs and chronic kidney disease must be excluded first, and they have been here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Injected insulin contains no precursor, so proinsulin and C-peptide would be normal or low rather than elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A meglitinide would stimulate endogenous secretion but would be detected on the sulfonylurea and meglitinide drug screen, which is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alcohol lowers glucose by raising NADH and blocking gluconeogenesis; insulin levels would be low, not markedly elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive hypoglycemia occurs 2 to 4 hours after meals, whereas his episodes occur in the morning and resolve with eating.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man without diabetes reports intermittent lightheadedness and sweating. A point-of-care meter at a health fair read 62 mg/dL while he felt well. Which of the following findings is required to establish a diagnosis of hypoglycemia in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low point-of-care glucose reading obtained while he is asymptomatic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Typical adrenergic symptoms after a meal with a normal glucose level

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fasting plasma glucose below 100 mg/dL on two separate mornings

choices.label: D
choices.text: Typical symptoms with a low plasma glucose, both relieved by glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: An elevated serum insulin level drawn when the glucose is normal

explanation.summary: Hypoglycemia is diagnosed by Whipple triad: low glucose, concurrent symptoms, and relief with glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Whipple triad requires documenting a low blood glucose at the same time as characteristic symptoms and then showing that both correct after glucose is given. In a patient without diabetes, the diagnosis rests on the triad with a reliable plasma measurement rather than a point-of-care value. A glucose of 70 mg/dL or below is the general-population alert value.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low reading without concurrent symptoms does not satisfy the triad, and point-of-care meters are not the reliable measurement required.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Postprandial symptoms without a documented glucose fall define idiopathic postprandial syndrome, not hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL is within the normal range and is not a diagnostic criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An insulin level drawn while glucose is normal is uninterpretable; these tests are done when the glucose is low.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and advanced chronic kidney disease has had increasingly frequent hypoglycemic episodes over the past 2 months, even though his insulin and glipizide doses have not changed. Which of the following best explains the increased frequency of his episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased renal clearance of insulin and oral antihyperglycemic drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased renal gluconeogenesis suppressing hepatic glucose output

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased hepatic glycogenolysis depleting circulating glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess cortisol secretion from stimulation of the adrenal cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid small intestinal glucose absorption after each meal

explanation.summary: Chronic kidney disease predisposes to hypoglycemia largely because insulin and oral agents are renally cleared.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin is cleared by the kidney, so falling filtration lets both prescribed insulin and oral antihyperglycemic drugs accumulate at unchanged doses. Renal gluconeogenesis, which normally contributes to glucose production, also falls as the kidney fails. Anorexia in advanced kidney disease reduces caloric intake and compounds the problem.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal gluconeogenesis decreases rather than increases in chronic kidney disease, and it does not suppress hepatic glucose output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogenolysis raises blood glucose; increasing it would protect against, not cause, hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol raises glucose, so excess cortisol would produce hyperglycemia; it is cortisol deficiency that causes hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rapid intestinal absorption underlies postprandial reactive hypoglycemia after GI surgery, which he has not had.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is found unresponsive at home with a plasma glucose of 34 mg/dL. Her family reports she was confused and irritable beforehand. Which of the following best explains why the brain is especially vulnerable to a fall in blood glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neurons require insulin in order to take up any glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Astrocytic glycogen sustains neurons for several days of fasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurons store almost no fuel and depend on circulating glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: The brain preferentially oxidizes free fatty acids for its energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons are entirely unable to use ketone bodies as a substrate

explanation.summary: The brain has negligible fuel stores and relies on a continuous supply of circulating glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurons hold essentially no glucose of their own, and the small astrocytic glycogen pool provides only a brief buffer. Because supply must therefore come continuously from the blood, a falling glucose level rapidly impairs cognition and can progress to coma. Ketone bodies only become a meaningful alternative substrate during prolonged fasting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Brain glucose uptake is not insulin dependent; vulnerability comes from the absence of stored fuel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Astrocytic glycogen buffers the brain only briefly, not for days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free fatty acids released by epinephrine-driven lipolysis serve other tissues; the brain runs on glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ketone bodies can serve as an alternative brain substrate, but only after prolonged fasting, so they do not help acutely.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes notices tremor, palpitations, anxiety, and hunger when her continuous glucose monitor reads 57 mg/dL, prompting her to eat. Action of which of the following hormones is most directly responsible for these warning symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucagon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin

explanation.summary: The adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia are produced by epinephrine released as glucose falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: As glucose drops toward the mid-50s, sympathoadrenal activation releases epinephrine from the adrenal gland. Its sympathetic effects produce tachycardia, sweating, tremor, anxiety, hunger, and dizziness, the classic fight-or-flight warning findings. Epinephrine also stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and drives adipose lipolysis to spare glucose for the brain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucagon is a counterregulatory hormone that raises glucose through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, but it does not generate the sympathetic warning symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol acts to raise glucose levels over a longer time course and does not produce acute adrenergic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth hormone also opposes insulin and raises glucose, but it does not cause tremor and palpitations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin lowers glucose; it is the hormone being counterregulated, not the source of these symptoms.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin is brought to the emergency department obtunded and unable to follow commands. His fingerstick glucose is 32 mg/dL and a confirmatory plasma glucose is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Have him drink fruit juice and eat crackers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start oral acarbose with his next meal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Begin a low-dose intravenous insulin infusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Admit him for a supervised 72-hour fast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Give intravenous dextrose without delay

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hypoglycemia with altered mental status is treated immediately with intravenous dextrose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most important step in any symptomatic patient is prompt correction of the glucose to avoid irreversible neurologic damage. Patients with altered mental status cannot take oral sugar safely, so intravenous dextrose is used; ready-to-use intranasal or injectable glucagon is an alternative when IV access is unavailable. Treatment should not wait for the confirmatory plasma value.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral juice, soda, milk, honey, or candy is appropriate only for a patient who is alert enough to swallow safely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acarbose is used for resistant reactive hypoglycemia and does nothing for an acute severe episode.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin would lower his glucose further and is contraindicated in hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A supervised fast is a diagnostic test for unexplained fasting hypoglycemia, and fasting him now would be dangerous.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman who underwent partial gastrectomy 2 years ago has tachycardia, sweating, and tremor roughly 3 hours after meals, with documented glucose values in the 50s mg/dL. Despite 4 months of frequent small meals, avoidance of refined sugar, and increased physical activity, her episodes persist. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Start acarbose to delay intestinal carbohydrate absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start glyburide to stabilize her postprandial glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add refined simple sugars to the start of each meal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Begin scheduled subcutaneous insulin before each meal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perform a supervised 72-hour fast to confirm the cause

explanation.summary: Reactive hypoglycemia that resists dietary change is treated with an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor such as acarbose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her postprandial symptoms follow upper GI surgery, in which rapid glucose transit produces an exaggerated insulin response. Acarbose and miglitol inhibit intestinal brush-border alpha-glucosidases and delay carbohydrate digestion and absorption. Blunting the postprandial glucose spike blunts the insulin surge that drives the later hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glyburide is a sulfonylurea that increases insulin secretion and would worsen her hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Limiting rather than adding refined sugar is advised, since simple sugars amplify the glucose and insulin spike.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin lowers glucose and would aggravate postprandial hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fast is for unexplained fasting hypoglycemia; her episodes are postprandial and already documented.

questions.topicName: Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man without diabetes reports 3 months of morning confusion and sweating that resolve after breakfast. He takes no medications and does not drink alcohol. Creatinine, liver enzymes, morning cortisol, TSH, and free T4 are all normal, and an office glucose drawn after lunch is 96 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Supervised mixed meal test with hourly glucose for 5 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin A1c measured on a fasting morning specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Supervised 72-hour fast with glucose and insulin every 6 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random growth hormone level drawn at the office visit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat point-of-care glucose meter check after each meal

explanation.summary: Unexplained fasting hypoglycemia is confirmed with a supervised 72-hour fast.
explanation.whyCorrect: His symptoms occur in the morning before eating, which is the fasting pattern. When the diagnosis is unclear after initial testing, a supervised 72-hour fast is performed with blood glucose and insulin checked every 6 hours until symptoms occur or the glucose drops below 55 mg/dL. Sampling during the low glucose is what makes the insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide results interpretable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mixed meal test is used for suspected reactive, postprandial hypoglycemia, and it has also been criticized as poorly reproducible.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin A1c reflects average glycemia and does not capture or confirm intermittent hypoglycemic episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A random growth hormone level is not diagnostic; suspected deficiency requires a GH stimulation test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postprandial meter checks target the wrong timing and would not provide the reliable plasma measurement needed.
